title: Check yourself: default constructors and this()

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A class declares no constructor at all. What does the page say happens when code writes `new` for it?

options.text: Java supplies a no-argument constructor, and fields get default values
options.says: The page says Java provides a default no-argument constructor that calls super(), and fields start at 0, null or false.

options.text: Java refuses to compile the class until a constructor is written for it
options.says: The page says a default constructor is provided, so the class compiles.

options.text: Java supplies a constructor taking one argument for every declared field
options.says: The provided constructor takes no arguments; field-by-field constructors are what records generate, not plain classes.

questions.stem: Where may a `this(...)` call go inside a constructor, according to the page?

options.text: Only as the very last statement in the body
options.says: The page requires it first, before any other statement, not last.

options.text: At any point, provided that it runs just once
options.says: Position matters: the page says it must be the first statement.

options.text: Only as the very first statement in the body
options.says: The page says the this() call must be the first statement in the constructor body.

concepts: With no constructor declared, Java supplies a no-argument one and fields start at their default values.
A this(...) call must be the first statement of a constructor.
